clinician.trajectory_summary: An 18-year-old male was admitted to the hospital after a motor vehicle accident with chief complaint of chest pain. Physical examination revealed limited chest movement, decreased tactile vocal fremitus on the right side, dullness upon percussion over the right area, and decreased breath sounds on the right side, with stable vital signs and normal oxygen saturation. CT chest with contrast revealed a large (13 × 23 × 15 cm) predominantly fat-containing mass with soft tissue components originating from the anterior mediastinum and extending into the right hemithorax, causing right lower lobe collapse without significant mediastinal shift. The patient underwent right thoracotomy with complete excision of the mass. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of thymolipoma, demonstrating an encapsulated lesion comprising mature adipose tissue with islands of non-neoplastic thymic epithelial cells. The patient experienced no postoperative complications and was discharged in excellent condition on postoperative day 11.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Large anterior mediastinal mass with imaging characteristics consistent with thymolipoma
Histopathological confirmation of thymolipoma: encapsulated mature adipose tissue with islands of non-neoplastic thymic epithelial cells
Right-sided physical exam findings (decreased fremitus, dullness, decreased breath sounds) explained by mass effect and right lower lobe collapse
Surgical treatment with complete excision via right thoracotomy
Successful post-operative course with no complications and discharge in excellent condition

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: CT imaging showed a well-defined, encapsulated fat-containing mass rather than acute blood or air collection; imaging characteristics and histopathology consistent with chronic benign lesion
Histopathology showed mature adipose tissue with non-neoplastic thymic epithelial cells, consistent with benign thymolipoma rather than malignancy
Histopathology demonstrated predominantly lipomatous composition with non-neoplastic thymic epithelium, characteristic of thymolipoma rather than thymic hyperplasia or thymoma

Whether the motor vehicle accident was truly coincidental or if the large mediastinal mass may have contributed to the trauma circumstances
Long-term follow-up imaging or clinical assessment post-discharge
